opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to the fact that robotics has historically been a very fragmented field. If you were a traditional roboticist, you'd often work in a lab with your own custom hardware, your own software stack, your own datasets that nobody else could really use. Every group was reinventing the wheel. And it was hard to compare results, hard to build on someone else's work, because reproducing it meant rebuilding their whole setup.

What we saw in the machine learning world, especially with NLP and transformers, was that once you have shared tools, shared models, shared datasets, progress accelerates enormously. People could take a model someone else trained, fine-tune it, share it back. That open loop is what made the field move so fast. And I think roboticists looked at that and thought, "Why don't we have this?"

So when LeRobot came along with a common format for datasets, pretrained policies you could actually download and run, and support for low-cost hardware, it lowered the barrier a lot. Suddenly you didn't need a hundred-thousand-dollar arm to contribute. You could build something for a few hundred dollars, collect data, share it on the Hub, and someone on the other side of the world could train on it.

There's also a shift in the methods themselves. Many traditional roboticists come from control theory, motion planning, very model-based approaches. Now there's this wave of learning-based methods: imitation learning, diffusion policies, vision-language-action models. Even people who are skeptical are curious, and they want a place where they can experiment without spending six months building infrastructure. I think LeRobot gives them that playground.

And honestly, the community itself is a big draw. People bring real expertise in hardware and control that the ML folks often lack, and the ML folks bring the data and modeling side. Bringing those two worlds together is, I think, where the really interesting progress will happen.

r001.rationale: The response describes conventional robotics as fragmented, with custom software stacks that make comparison and reproduction difficult, then connects the appeal of shared learning tools and learning-based methods to that problem.

r002.rationale: The response says low-cost hardware lowers barriers to contribution, but does not attribute labs’ robot adoption to robots being an accessible entry point for students.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what we're seeing is actually quite similar to what happened in NLP around 2018, 2019. If you remember, back then a lot of the people doing natural language processing were very much from a linguistics background, very specialized, with their own tools and their own ways of doing things. And then transformers arrived, and suddenly you had this big wave of people coming from deep learning, from computer vision, who were just saying, "Okay, I'll take this big model, I'll train it on a lot of data, and let's see what happens." And the two communities kind of had to meet.

Robotics today feels a lot like that. Traditional roboticists have decades of really deep knowledge: control theory, kinematics, planning, how to deal with real hardware that breaks and drifts and has latency. That knowledge is extremely valuable, and honestly, a lot of the people coming from the AI side don't have it. So when they join LeRobot, I don't think it's because they feel their field is being replaced. I think it's more that they see something interesting happening, that end-to-end learning is starting to work on real robots, and they want to be part of it rather than watching from the outside.

And the other thing that draws them, I think, is the open-source aspect. Robotics has historically been a quite closed field. Every lab had its own stack, its own simulator, its own data format, and reproducing someone else's result was almost impossible. The kind of culture we tried to bring with Transformers, where you have one shared library, shared datasets, shared pretrained models, and anyone can download and run the same thing in a few lines of code, that's something many roboticists were craving for years but never really had. So when they come to LeRobot, it's partly for the models, but it's really a lot for the community and the standardization. They can share a dataset, someone across the world can train on it, and they can compare results. That's new for them.

So my understanding is it's a mix of curiosity about what deep learning can bring, a bit of pragmatism because they can see where the field is going, and really a desire for the open, collaborative way of working that was just missing in robotics. And for us it's great, because they bring the hardware expertise and the realism that keep the project grounded, and we bring the tooling and the ML side. The combination is much stronger than either one alone.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics had closed, fragmented software stacks and that roboticists wanted shared tools and easier reproducibility, attributing some of their interest to those constraints.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention academic labs, students, or robots serving as an accessible entry point.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of traditional roboticists are curious about what this new wave of machine learning can bring to robotics. They have a huge amount of experience with the hardware, with control, with all the things that make a robot actually work in the real world. But getting started with learning-based approaches can still be quite difficult. You need data, you need implementations, and you need a way to compare what you’re doing with what other people are doing.

So I think the attraction of LeRobot is having a shared place to do that. You don’t have to build the entire stack yourself before you can start experimenting. And it goes both ways: the machine learning community has a lot to learn from roboticists. Bringing those communities together is a big part of the opportunity.

r001.rationale: The response says traditional roboticists are curious about machine learning and may find learning-based approaches difficult to start, but it does not attribute their interest to frustration with constraints of conventional robotics software.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention academic labs, students, or robots serving as an accessible entry point for students.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of traditional roboticists are excited because they see an opportunity to build on what other people are doing much more easily. Robotics has historically been quite fragmented: you have your robot, your software stack, your dataset, and it takes a lot of work to reproduce someone else’s results.

With LeRobot, the idea is to have a common place where you can share datasets, share models, and try them on real hardware. You don’t have to start from scratch every time. And that brings together people with very complementary expertise. Traditional roboticists understand the hardware, control, and all the things that become difficult when you move into the physical world. People coming from machine learning bring experience training models and working with large datasets. I think the interest is really in what those communities can build together.

r001.rationale: The response describes fragmented robotics software and the difficulty of reproducing results, but attributes interest in LeRobot to sharing work and combining expertise; it does not clearly say traditional roboticists are interested in AI because they are frustrated with conventional robotics software constraints.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention academic labs adopting robots or robots providing students with an accessible entry point.
